topic: SIPRI Report: India as 2nd Largest Arms Importer

subtopics.title: SIPRI and global arms transfers
subtopics.summary: The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), an independent research institute, released the Trends in International Arms Transfers 2025 report on global defence trade. International arms transfers rose 9.2% in 2021-25 compared with 2016-20. The rise in European arms imports, up 210%, was largely driven by the Russia-Ukraine war.
facts: SIPRI: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, established 1966
SIPRI headquarters: Stockholm, Sweden
SIPRI focus areas: Conflict and Peace Studies; Armaments and Military Expenditure; Arms Transfers and Disarmament
International arms transfers rose 9.2% (2021-25 vs 2016-20)
Arms imports by European countries rose 210%
Rise in European imports largely driven by the Russia-Ukraine war

subtopics.title: Top global exporters and importers
subtopics.summary: The SIPRI report ranks the largest arms exporters and importers for 2021-25. The United States led exports with a 42% share, while Ukraine topped imports with a 9.7% share. Russia's arms exports fell sharply, cutting its share of global exports.
facts: Top exporter: United States, 42% share
Next exporters in order: France, Russia, Germany, China
Russia's arms exports declined by 64%
Russia's share of global exports fell to 6.8%
Top importer: Ukraine, 9.7% share
India ranked second among importers, with an 8.2% share

subtopics.title: India as 2nd largest arms importer
subtopics.summary: India remained the second-largest arms importer during 2021-25, with an 8.2% share. Its overall arms imports fell by 4%, largely due to increased domestic defence manufacturing and indigenisation. Russia, France and Israel were its main suppliers.
facts: India's import rank in 2021-25: 2nd largest
India's share of global arms imports: 8.2%
India's overall arms imports declined by 4%
Decline largely due to domestic manufacturing and indigenisation efforts
India's supplier composition: Russia 40%
India's supplier composition: France 29%
India's supplier composition: Israel 15%

subtopics.title: India's push for domestic defence
subtopics.summary: India has set production and export targets for 2029 and is building its domestic defence capacity. Policy changes, defence industrial corridors and foreign investment rules support this aim. The top three export destinations are the US, France and Armenia.

quizzes.passage: International arms transfers are the movement of weapons and military equipment from one country to another, and they show how global defence trade is changing. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, an independent research body that studies conflict and peace, armaments, military expenditure and disarmament, examined these transfers in its Trends in International Arms Transfers 2025 report. The report analysed the period from 2021 to 2025 and compared it with the earlier five-year period from 2016 to 2020, which allows changes in global defence trade to be measured over time. Its findings show that overall transfers grew between the two periods. The increase was particularly strong in Europe, where arms imports rose sharply, and the institute linked much of this surge to the Russia-Ukraine war. Trade patterns also shifted among suppliers, as one major exporter saw its shipments fall significantly and its share of global exports became much smaller. The report offers a picture of which countries supply weapons to the world and which countries buy them. Such information helps observers understand how the balance of global defence trade is moving. Because the report looks at both exporting and importing countries, it gives a balanced view of the market, showing which states sell arms abroad and which states acquire them for their own forces. The analysis also places the transfers within the institute's wider focus on armaments and military expenditure.

quizzes.passage: India has long been one of the largest buyers of defence equipment in the world, and its purchases shape both its military capability and its relationships with foreign suppliers. In the most recent SIPRI assessment, covering 2021 to 2025, India kept a high position among the world's arms importers. However, its total arms imports during this period were lower than in the earlier phase, a change linked to a growing push for domestic production. Over the past several years, the government has focused on building a stronger defence manufacturing base at home. Procurement policy was revised to prioritise Indian-made products over foreign purchases, which signals a clear preference for local industry. To support this shift, industrial corridors have been created in certain states to bring together manufacturers and suppliers. Foreign investment is also allowed in the defence sector through both automatic and government routes, while a dedicated initiative supports start-ups and small firms working on innovation. Taken together, these steps aim to reduce dependence on imported weapons and to turn India into a larger producer and exporter of defence equipment. The way procurement rules are designed determines how much equipment is sourced from abroad and how much is built locally. Industry players are being encouraged to take on more of the manufacturing work, which supports the aim of building a broader defence industrial base.
